אפי' אם שטר החוב בידו. ע' בת' עבוה"ג סימן ע' בענין ראובן שעשה איזה עסק עם שמעון דהיינו ששמעון חייב א"ע להמציא לראובן איזה סחורה וראובן התחייב א"ע לקבל הסחורות ולשלם תמורתן והעמיד ראובן את לוי לע"ק בעדו נגד שמעון לשלם לו תמורת הסחור' וראובן עשה שטר פיצוי ללוי לפצותו ולב"כ שלא יהי' להם היזק וגר"ה כו' גם נכתב בש"פ נאמנות כנהוג וכל זמן ששטר פיצוי זה קיים בדלא נכתב עליו תברא אין אני נאמן עליו לומר מפוצה מסולק פרוע מחילה רבית הוא ולא שום טענה בעולם אדרבא לוי וב"כ נאמנים כו' ויד בעל השטר על העליונה כו' והנה לוי בירר בבירור גמור שהוא שילם לשמעון בעד בסחורה שמסר לראובן לכן תובע לוי לראובן שיחזיר לו מעותיו וראובן השיב שקודם שפרע לוי לשמעון נתן הוא המעות ליד לוי שיתנם לשמעון גם טען ראובן שנודע לו אחר התחייבות פיצוי הנ"ל שלוי הי' שותף עם שמעון בסחור' הנ"ל ולוי השיב מה לך נ"ח אם הייתי שותף או לא. והנה דעת הרב השואל בפשוט שהדין עם לוי וחנם אחד חלק עליו וסבירא ליה שהשטר פיצוי בטל שהרי ממעטינן בענין נאמנות דאינו קאי אלא על פרעון ולא על שאר דברים (כבסימן ע"א ס"ג) לכן נאמן ראובן לומר' שהוא נתן המעות ללוי ליתנם לשמעון. והוא ז"ל השיב שהנכון עם הרב השואל שהדין עם לוי דמ"ש שכנגדו הנ"ל שהרי ממעטינן בענין נאמנות לכאורה אין טעם זה מספיק אלא שלא יהא לוי נאמן בלא שבועה אבל לבטל הש"פ לגמרי אין כאן אפי' דמות ראי' וא"ל דכוונתו כשם שממעטינן בענין נאמנות שאינו קאי אלא על הפרעון כן יש לנו לומר ג"כ על הש"פ בכלל שאינו אמור אלא אם יתברר ששילם לוי לשמעון מעות שלו רק ראובן יאמר שא"כ החזיר לו מעותיו אזי חל הש"פ עם כל תוקף של הנאמנות אבל אם יפול הפרש ביניהם אם שילם לוי מכיסו על זה לא נעשה הש"פ כלל זה אינו דשטר פיצוי הוא העיקר לפצות את לוי שלא יתבע שמעון המעות כלל כי פיצוי הוא ל' הצלה כמו פצני והצילני Even if the debt instrument is in his possession. Responsa Avodat HaGershuni, siman 70, discusses a business arrangement in which Shimon undertook to supply merchandise to Reuven, Reuven undertook to accept it and pay, and Reuven appointed Levi as an arev kablan for the price. Reuven gave Levi a comprehensive indemnity deed containing the usual strong ne'emanut clause, stating that so long as the deed remained uncancelled Reuven would not be believed to claim that Levi had been indemnified, released, paid, forgiven, or to raise any other defense, while Levi and his representatives would be believed and the holder of the deed would have the upper hand. Levi later proved conclusively that he had paid Shimon for the merchandise delivered to Reuven and demanded reimbursement. Reuven answered that before Levi paid Shimon he had already given Levi the money to transmit, and also claimed that he later discovered that Levi had been Shimon's partner in the merchandise. The responsum analyzes whether the ne'emanut clause is limited to a claim of payment or extends to these defenses, and whether Reuven can be believed against the indemnity deed. Its conclusion is that the strong language of the deed and the circumstances of the proven payment give Levi the superior claim, subject to the detailed rules of ne'emanut and the precise wording of the instrument. See there at length.
Even if the debt document is in his possession. See Responsa Avodat HaGershuni, siman 70, concerning Reuven, who entered a business arrangement with Shimon. Shimon undertook to supply certain merchandise to Reuven, and Reuven undertook to accept it and pay for it. Reuven appointed Levi as a kablan guarantor toward Shimon to pay for the merchandise, and Reuven gave Levi an indemnity document obligating himself to reimburse Levi and his representatives so that they would suffer no loss or indirect damage. The indemnity document also contained the customary clause of trustworthiness: so long as the document remains in force and no receipt is written upon it, Reuven is not believed to say that Levi was reimbursed, released, paid, waived the claim, that the transaction involved interest, or any other claim; rather, Levi and his representatives are believed, and the holder of the document has the stronger hand. Levi proved conclusively that he had paid Shimon for the merchandise delivered to Reuven and therefore demanded reimbursement from Reuven. Reuven answered that before Levi paid Shimon, he himself had given the money to Levi to deliver to Shimon. Reuven also claimed that after making the indemnity obligation he discovered that Levi had been Shimon's partner in the merchandise. Levi answered: what difference does it make whether I was a partner or not? The questioning rabbi assumed that Levi should prevail. Another scholar disagreed and argued that the indemnity document was ineffective because the law limits clauses of trustworthiness to repayment and not to other matters, as in siman 71, seif 3. Therefore, he argued, Reuven should be believed to say that he gave the money to Levi to deliver to Shimon. Avodat HaGershuni answered that the questioning rabbi was correct and Levi prevails. The other scholar's argument concerning the limitation of trustworthiness might show only that Levi is not believed without an oath; it offers no basis to annul the indemnity document entirely. Nor can one say that just as trustworthiness is limited to repayment, the entire indemnity was intended to apply only if it were established that Levi paid Shimon from his own money, while disputes over whether Levi paid from his own pocket would fall outside the document. The very essence of an indemnity is to protect Levi so that Shimon will not extract money from him. The word "indemnify" denotes rescue and protection. Thus Reuven obligated himself to save Levi from Shimon's claim, and the clause of trustworthiness applies to that obligation. Avodat HaGershuni notes that he is aware of Responsa Maharshal, siman 93, concerning two people who borrowed under one document, where one later paid the document, obtained it, and sued the other for his share. The other said, "I already paid you my portion so that you could pay the entire debt." Maharshal ruled that the defendant swears and is exempt. One might therefore think the borrower here is also believed to say he already paid the guarantor. In truth, however, that case proves the opposite. Maharshal's reasoning was that the debtor could not say, "Why is your document in my opponent's hand?" First, the single debt document had until then remained in the creditor's possession. Second, even if the document were in the co borrower's possession, it did not create a lien by one co borrower against the other; it merely recorded that both were jointly obligated. Here, neither reason applies. The document is in the guarantor's possession, and it is itself a lien from the borrower to the guarantor. Therefore the borrower is certainly not believed to say he had paid earlier. Beyond this, Avodat HaGershuni raises additional difficulties in Maharshal's proof from Baal HaTerumot. See the Sema, siman 77, seif katan 27, and what is written there. In the present case, even Maharshal agrees that Reuven is not believed to say he paid previously. As to Reuven's further claim that the indemnity should be void because Levi had been Shimon's partner, Avodat HaGershuni says he cannot rule either way because Reuven never explained why this partnership should annul the indemnity. What benefit or difference would it create if Levi had not been Shimon's partner? These are his words. See there. See also Noda B'Yehudah, second edition, siman 13, concerning this.

אפי' אם הש"ח בידו. עיין בסמ"ע ס"ק י"ג עד כנ"ל בביאור הטור והמחבר והבעה"ת ולא כמ"ש בע"ש שגם כשכתב לו התקבלתי לא מהני כו' עכ"ל סמ"ע אמת שכן מוכח בטור ובריב"ש סי' קע"ח אבל בבעה"ת לא מוכח מידי דהא אדרבה משמע שם איפכא וכמו שאכתוב לקמן וגם ברמב"ם ומחבר לא מוכח מידי ודוק וגם מ"ש הסמ"ע וכ"כ המ"מ פכ"ו דמלוה בהדיא בפשיטות כו' וכיון למגיד משנה שהביא לקמן סי' קל"א (ס"ג) [סק"ג] ולפע"ד אדרב' משמע משם להפך דדוקא כשכתב התקבלתי ונתן לו זכותו דהיינו שהקנה לוהשטר בכתיבה ומסירה באופן שנתבאר לעיל סי' (פ"ו) [ס"ו] הא לאו הכי יכול לטעון פרעתיך והיינו דמסיים המ"מ ופשוט הוא דלא יגרע כח הערב מאינש נכרי דעלמא כו' ואי בהתקבלתי לחוד ודאי לא סגי באיש נכרי דעלמא אלא בקניות שטרות ממש וכן פי' הב"ח דברי הר"ן שהביא הב"י דדוקא כשכתב לו התקבלתי ונתן לו זכותו בכתיב' ומסירה והוא נכון וכן משמע מדברי נ"י פרק חזקת הבתים וכן כתב הב"ח בשם חדושי רשב"א פ' גט פשוט דבהתקבלתי לחוד מצי למימ' פרעתיך ור"ל חדושי רמב"ן כי כן היא שם (מיהו מ"ש הב"ח שגם דעת התוספות כן אינו מוכרח ע"ש ודוק) וכן דעת מהרש"ל בתשו' סי' צ"ג דאפילו ידוע שפרע הערב יכול הלוה לומר לו פרעתיך והב"ח בס"ס ע"ז כתב עליו דלא דק דבהתקבלתי פשיטא דגובה בו כמבואר להדיא בפ' ג"פ דף קע"ד כו' והוא לא דק וסותר דברי עצמו שהביא כאן כמה פוסקים דסוברים כמהרש"ל ומפ' ג"פ אין ראיה די"ל דמיירי בשהקנה לו השטר וכמו שפיר' הבעה"ת שער ל"ה ח"ב ושאר פוסקים וכן משמע דמפרש רי"ו נכ"ו ח"ג א"נ התקבלתי דהתם פירושו שהלוה כתב לערב הריני כאלו התקבלתי ממך המעות וכמו שפירשו בעל המאור ותוספות שם וראב"ן סי' ס"ח וכן פי' בתשו' רשב"א סי' תתפ"ח הלכך נראה דלענין דינא הממע"ה. שוב ראיתי בר"י נתיב ה' כתב להדיא דיכול לטעון פרעתי אפילו כתב לו התקבלתי אם לא שהקנהו לו בכתיבה ומסירה ע"ש וכן ראיתי בתשו' מבי"ט ח"ב ס"ס ר"ך דף ק"ד ע"א מסיק כן בשם הרשב"א בשם רבו ה"ר יונה ובשם הפוסקים דדוקא כשכתב לו התקבלתי והקנה לו השטר בכתיבה ומסירה הוא דאינו יכול לומר פרעתיך אבל בהתקבלתי לחוד מצי למימר פרעתיך ומסכים שם המבי"ט לדבריהם ושוב מצאתי בתשובת מהרא"ן ששון סי' ע' שמפרש דברי הר"ן והמ"מ כמו שכתבתי וס"ל לדינא אע"ג שכתב לו התקבלתי יכול לטעון פרעתיך ע"ש וקרוב אלי לומר דגם ה"ר יונה בהרא"ש פ' חז"ה מיירי בהתקבלתי (אבל בטור א"א לפרש כן דא"כ למה כתב שצריך שהוזכר הערבות בשטר וגם למה כ' שאינו טורף ממשועבדים הא פשיטא כיון שכתב לו התקבלתי דהיינו שהקנה לו בכתיבה ומסירה אפי' היה אינש דעלמא שאינו ערב טורף ממשועבדים) ונתן לו זכותו וכמ"ש הרשב"א בשמו וקיצר במובן וכן משמע מלשונו שם שכתב דאם לא כן יכול הלוה לטעון כו' או שמא הוא מסר לך שטר זה ואין אותיות ניקנות במסירה כו' ולפ"ז אתי שפיר מ"ש הרא"ש וה"ר יונה פירש כו' כלומר דלפי פירוש ה"ר יונה אין צריך לומר שנזכר הערבות בשטר וכן משמע להדיא בר' ירוחם נתיב ה' דהר' יונה מיירי שכתב לו התקבלתי ונתן לו כתיבה ומסירה ע"ש רק מ"ש ברי"ו ופי' הר"י ט"ס הוא וצ"ל וה"ר יונה פי' ולא כהטור סי' זה וברמזיו פ' חזקת חבתים שהבין דגם לה"ר יונה צריך לומר שנזכר הערבות בשטר ע"ש ודו"ק. וע"ש הב"ח דבהר"י שבהרא"ש י"ל דלא קאמר אלא שא"י לטעון שמא לא פרעתי למלוה אבל אה"נ דיכול לטעון פרעתיך כו' לא עיין בש"ס ובהרא"ש כלל (רק בב"י שהביא בקיצור דברי הרא"ש בשם ה"ר יונה) דהא איתא התם דהלוה א"ל פרעתיך ואינו נאמן ע"ש אלא ודאי כדפי' ודוק. ולפ"ז נ"ל ברור דה"ה כשמביא הערב עדים שפרע יכול הלוה לומר Even if the debt instrument is in his possession. The Sema explains that this is the correct understanding of the Tur, Mechaber, and Baal HaTerumot, unlike the Levush, who says that even a written acknowledgment of receipt does not help. It is true that the Tur and Rivash, siman 178, imply the Sema’s view, but nothing is proved from the Baal HaTerumot. On the contrary, his words imply the opposite, as I shall explain. Nor is anything proved from the Rambam or Mechaber. The Sema also cites the Maggid Mishneh as explicit support, but in my humble opinion the Maggid Mishneh implies the opposite: only where the lender wrote an acknowledgment of receipt and transferred his right, meaning that he assigned the debt instrument through writing and delivery in the manner explained above in siman 66, may the borrower no longer plead that he paid the guarantor. Otherwise, the borrower may say, ‘I paid you.’ This is why the Maggid Mishneh concludes that the guarantor’s position cannot be weaker than that of an unrelated purchaser. A mere acknowledgment of receipt would certainly not suffice for an unrelated purchaser without a full assignment of the instrument. The Bach correctly explains the Ran cited by the Beit Yosef in the same way, namely that the lender wrote an acknowledgment and transferred his right by writing and delivery. Nimukei Yosef in Chezkat HaBatim implies the same. The Bach also cites the novellae of the Rashba to Get Pashut as holding that a mere acknowledgment does not prevent the borrower from pleading payment; the work meant is in fact the Ramban’s novellae. Maharshal, Responsa siman 93, likewise rules that even if it is known that the guarantor paid, the borrower may say, ‘I paid you.’ The Bach later objects that an acknowledgment plainly permits recovery, but this contradicts the authorities he himself cites here. Get Pashut supplies no proof, for it may concern a case in which the debt instrument was assigned by writing and delivery, as explained by the Baal HaTerumot and other authorities. Alternatively, the ‘acknowledgment’ there may mean that the borrower wrote to the guarantor, ‘I regard myself as though I received the money from you,’ as explained by Baal HaMaor, Tosafot, Raavan, and the Rashba. Rabbenu Yerucham states expressly that even if the lender wrote an acknowledgment, the borrower may plead payment unless the debt instrument was transferred by writing and delivery. Responsa Mabit likewise concludes in the name of the Rashba, Rabbenu Yonah, and other authorities that only an acknowledgment combined with assignment by writing and delivery bars the plea of payment. R. Aharon Sasson also explains the Ran and Maggid Mishneh this way and rules accordingly. It is also likely that Rabbenu Yonah, cited by the Rosh in Chezkat HaBatim, refers to an acknowledgment together with transfer of the right, as the Rashba reports in his name. The Tur cannot be interpreted that way, because the Tur separately requires that the guarantee be mentioned in the instrument and says that the guarantor may not collect from encumbered property. If the document had been fully assigned to him, even an unrelated purchaser could collect from encumbered property. Rabbenu Yerucham expressly understands Rabbenu Yonah to require acknowledgment and assignment by writing and delivery. The Bach’s suggestion that Rabbenu Yonah merely bars the borrower from saying that perhaps the guarantor did not pay, while still allowing him to plead that he later paid the guarantor, is impossible, for the Gemara and Rosh expressly address a borrower who says, ‘I paid you,’ and reject that plea. According to what has been explained, it is clear that even where the guarantor brings witnesses that he paid the lender, the borrower may still say to the guarantor, ‘I later paid you.’ If a written acknowledgment does not defeat that plea, witnesses to the guarantor’s payment certainly do not, for a litigant’s admission is equivalent to one hundred witnesses. The Tur’s contrary ruling follows his own view that a mere acknowledgment bars the plea of payment. The Levush is inconsistent: after ruling that a mere acknowledgment does not bar the plea, he nevertheless follows the Tur where witnesses prove the guarantor’s payment. The Ramban’s novellae to Get Pashut state explicitly that when the guarantor sues the borrower, if there are no witnesses that the guarantor paid, the borrower may plainly say, ‘I paid you.’ Even if witnesses prove that the guarantor paid the lender, the guarantor may recover only if it is also known that the borrower did not thereafter pay the guarantor. Similarly, if the lender wrote an acknowledgment, the borrower may still say that he later paid the guarantor, since the guarantor’s claim against him is not itself a documented loan. Nimukei Yosef and the Baal HaTerumot imply the same. The Baal HaTerumot writes that the guarantor must prove that he paid, but if he brings no proof, or if the borrower pleads, ‘I paid you,’ the borrower is believed, and the instrument in the guarantor’s possession does not convert the claim into a documented loan. His proof from the Mishna’s phrase ‘If he wrote him an acknowledgment, he collects’ concerns an acknowledgment joined with assignment by writing and delivery. Otherwise, even proof that the guarantor paid would not bar the borrower from claiming that he later paid the guarantor. This is the correct practical ruling.

(Seif 3) If the lender wrote. Sema writes that when witnesses saw the guarantor pay the lender, no written receipt is required. This is difficult. Even if witnesses prove payment to the lender, why should the borrower not be believed to say that he later repaid the guarantor, since the guarantor has no document establishing that debt? Moreover, these words come from Sefer HaTerumot, gate 35, which expressly says that even after the guarantor proves payment to the lender, if the borrower claims, “I paid you,” the borrower is believed. The original note in the guarantor's hands does not turn his reimbursement claim into a documented loan. The Tur's wording does not support Sema's reading. The Tur first says that without witnesses the guarantor collects nothing, even absent any claim of repayment. He then states a separate rule: even if the note is in the guarantor's hands, whether witnesses establish his payment and the borrower now claims repayment, or no witnesses exist and the borrower says that the lender was never paid, the guarantor does not collect unless the lender wrote a receipt. The Shulchan Aruch intends only to teach that possession of the original note does not itself prove that the guarantor paid.
